title: Multi-channel collective dissipation via the symmetric irreducible representation of SU(4)
authors: M. Lutsukh, M. Bazarsana, T. Begzjav, G. O. Ariunbold
abstract: We specialize Agarwal's multi-level collective spontaneous-emission formalism to the four-level case by formulating it in the fully symmetric \SU(4) representation of $N$ identical atoms. In the irreducible representation $(N,0,0)$, the occupation-number basis forms a tetrahedral weight lattice on which the six embedded $\mathfrak{su}(2)$ transition subalgebras act as ladder operators. From these algebraic factors we obtain a compact Pauli-type population-rate equation and a closed-form expression for the total emitted intensity that apply to any combination of open dipole channels. The formalism is then specialized to the seven dipole-allowed four-level topologies -- tripod, inverted tripod, Y, inverted Y, double-$Λ$, closed cascade, and diamond -- and the resulting rate equations are solved numerically for atom numbers up to $N=50$. In every case the emitted intensity develops a delayed cooperative burst whose peak height obeys a power law $I_{\mathrm{peak}}=aN^{p}$ with topology-dependent parameters $(a,p)$; the fitted exponents lie in the range $1.81\lesssim p\lesssim 1.92$, indicating a superlinear. The \SU(4) tetrahedral flow and the seven configuration-dependent transients together provide a unified geometric picture of multi-channel collective dissipation in four-level atomic ensembles.
summary: This paper unifies the theoretical description of collective spontaneous emission in four-level atomic ensembles using the mathematical framework of SU(4) symmetry. By solving derived Pauli rate equations for seven distinct physical topologies, the authors predict that the emitted light intensity will exhibit a delayed cooperative burst scaling superlinearly with atom number ($N^p$). This provides a comprehensive geometric and quantitative tool for studying multi-level quantum coherence.
main_problem: The work develops a unified theoretical framework for modeling multi-channel collective spontaneous emission in atomic ensembles containing four internal energy levels.
main_result: The emitted intensity exhibits a delayed cooperative burst whose peak height scales superlinearly with the number of atoms ($I_{	ext{peak}} \propto N^p$ with $1.81 \lesssim p \lesssim 1.92$).
method: The dynamics are derived by specializing Agarwal's multi-level formalism to the four-level case, utilizing the fully symmetric irreducible representation of SU(4) and solving resulting Pauli-type rate equations numerically.
model_or_system: The system consists of $N$ identical atoms with a four-level structure ($\mathcal{H}_1 \cong \mathbb{C}^4$). The collective dynamics are mapped onto the fully symmetric representation $(N, 0, 0)$ of SU(4), whose weight space forms a tetrahedral lattice.
key_observables: Total emitted intensity $I(t)$, peak emitted intensity ($I_{	ext{peak}}$), and time evolution of level populations $\langle q_k(t) angle/N$.
important_parameters: Atom number $N$ (up to 50); seven specific dipole-allowed four-level topologies (e.g., tripod, Y, diamond).
main_assumptions: The dynamics are governed by the diagonal part of the master equation, allowing for a closed Pauli-type rate equation description.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate $I(t)$ for various topologies at different $N$, confirm power-law scaling of $I_{	ext{peak}}$ vs $N^2$, and show normalized population dynamics across the seven studied configurations.
paper_structure: The paper establishes the SU(4) mathematical framework, derives the compact Pauli rate equation from the master equation, specializes this formalism to seven physical four-level topologies, solves these equations numerically for various N, and analyzes the resulting power-law scaling of the emitted intensity burst.
why_interesting: This work provides a powerful generalization of superradiance theory (Dicke/Agarwal) into higher symmetry groups (SU(4)), offering quantitative predictions for complex multi-level quantum emitters relevant to cavity QED and atomic physics experiments.
